name: Sun
description: The Sun is the star at the center of the Solar System. It is a nearly perfect sphere of hot plasma, with internal convective motion that generates a magnetic field via a dynamo process. The Sun radiates energy primarily through nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core.
magnetic_field: ~1 Gauss (average), up to 3,000 Gauss in sunspots
summary: The Sun is our nearest star and the engine of the Solar System. Through nuclear fusion, it converts 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium every second, releasing the energy that powers all life on Earth. The Sun's magnetic activity drives phenomena like sunspots, solar flares, and coronal mass ejections that affect space weather throughout the Solar System.
interesting_facts: The Sun converts 4 million tons of mass into energy every second through E=mc²
The Sun's core is hotter than 15 million degrees Celsius
The Sun accounts for 99.86% of all mass in the Solar System
Solar energy takes 100,000 years to travel from the core to the surface, then 8 minutes to reach Earth
The Sun has been shining for 4.6 billion years and has enough hydrogen for another 5 billion
The Sun will eventually become a red giant, expanding to engulf Mercury and Venus
Over 1 million Earths could fit inside the Sun
The Sun's corona (outer atmosphere) is mysteriously hotter than its surface
Solar flares can release energy equivalent to billions of nuclear bombs
The Sun completes one galactic orbit every 225–250 million years

faq.a: The Sun is a G-type main-sequence star (yellow dwarf) at the center of our Solar System, about 4.6 billion years old, providing the energy that powers all life on Earth through nuclear fusion.
The Sun's surface (photosphere) is about 5,778 K (5,505°C). Its core reaches 15 million°C. Paradoxically, the outer corona is 1–3 million°C, far hotter than the surface.

faq.q: How far is the Sun from Earth?
faq.a: The average distance is about 149.6 million km (1 Astronomical Unit). At this distance, sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth.
The Sun has a diameter of 1,392,700 km — about 109 times Earth's diameter. Over 1 million Earths could fit inside the Sun.

faq.q: What is the Sun made of?
faq.a: The Sun is composed primarily of hydrogen (73%) and helium (25%), with trace amounts of oxygen, carbon, iron, and other elements — typical composition for a star.

faq.q: How does the Sun produce energy?
faq.a: The Sun produces energy through nuclear fusion in its core, where hydrogen nuclei (protons) fuse together to form helium, releasing enormous amounts of energy described by Einstein's E=mc².
In about 5 billion years, the Sun will exhaust its hydrogen fuel and expand into a red giant, likely engulfing Mercury and Venus. It will then shed its outer layers, leaving behind a white dwarf.
Sunspots are temporary dark areas on the Sun's surface where strong magnetic fields inhibit convection, causing those regions to be cooler (about 3,500°C vs 5,500°C) and appear darker.
A solar flare is a sudden, intense burst of radiation from the Sun's surface, caused by the release of magnetic energy. They can disrupt radio communications and power grids on Earth.

faq.q: What spacecraft have visited the Sun?
faq.a: The Parker Solar Probe (NASA) is the closest human-made object to the Sun. Other missions include Solar Orbiter (ESA/NASA), SOHO, Ulysses, and Hinode which study the Sun from various distances.

The solar wind is a continuous stream of charged particles (mostly electrons and protons) flowing outward from the Sun at 400–800 km/s. It creates the heliosphere and interacts with planetary magnetic fields to produce auroras.

faq.q: What is a coronal mass ejection?
faq.a: A CME is a large expulsion of plasma and magnetic field from the Sun's corona. When directed at Earth, CMEs can cause geomagnetic storms, auroras, and potentially disrupt satellite and electrical systems.
